title: The V-2's first successful flight, 1942 — from vengeance weapon to the Moon
sources: Wikipedia: V-2 rocket — the fourth flight was the first successful test flight, on 3 October 1942, reaching 84.5 km; Walter Dornberger at Peenemünde: 'This third day of October, 1942, is the first of a new era in transportation, that of space travel'; on 22 December 1942 Hitler signed the order for mass production; built at the Mittelwerk by prisoners from Mittelbau-Dora, a concentration camp where 20,000 prisoners died; beginning in September 1944 more than 3,000 V-2s were launched against Allied targets, first London and later Antwerp and Liège; faster than sound, no warning; an estimated 2,754 civilians killed in London; more people died manufacturing the V-2 than were killed by its deployment

Wikipedia: Wernher von Braun — 22 December 1942 Hitler ordered the A-4 into production as a 'vengeance weapon'; surrendered to the US military (Operation Paperclip); chief architect of the Saturn V that propelled the Apollo spacecraft to the Moon
Wikipedia: Mittelwerk — the underground factory's tunnel system

Archive film (public domain, Wikimedia Commons): 'V-2 Rocket Assembling and Launching 1947' (captured V-2s at White Sands); '1946-11-21 White Sands NM V-2 rocket' (incl. film of Earth from a V-2 camera); NASA 'Flight of AS-506 (Apollo 11)'

Photos (public domain): V-weapons in the Mittelwerk tunnels, May 1945; Mittelwerk tunnel entrance, 1945 (US Army); Dornberger and von Braun after their surrender, 3 May 1945; V-2 damage in London, March 1945 (RAF); ruined flats in Limehouse; von Braun and the Apollo 11 Saturn V, July 1969 (NASA); first photo from space, V-2, 24 October 1946 (US Army)

post.facebook:
On this day in 1942, the V-2 rocket made its first successful flight, climbing 84.5 kilometres into the sky.

Its commander, Walter Dornberger, called 3 October 1942 "the first of a new era in transportation, that of space travel". Hitler saw something else: in December he ordered the rocket into production as a vengeance weapon.

V-2s were built in the tunnels of the Mittelwerk by prisoners from the Mittelbau-Dora concentration camp, where 20,000 prisoners died. From September 1944, more than 3,000 were fired — first at London, then at Antwerp and Liège. The rocket fell faster than sound, with no warning; in London alone it killed an estimated 2,754 people. More people died building the V-2 than were killed by it.

After the war, its designer Wernher von Braun surrendered to the Americans. In the United States he became the chief architect of the Saturn V — the rocket that carried Apollo to the Moon.
